subject: Career
title: The Six Causes of Burnout
description: A quick, practical guide to The Six Causes of Burnout.

hook.text: Most people blame overwork for burnout. But Maslach found six causes — and workload is just one of them.

buildup.text: The six: workload, control, reward, community, fairness, and values. Any mismatch can trigger burnout.

discovery.text: You can work reasonable hours but still burn out if you feel undervalued, powerless, or morally conflicted.

twist.text: The most common burnout cause isn't overwork — it's lack of control over how you do your job.

climax.text: Diagnose your burnout source: is it volume, autonomy, recognition, belonging, fairness, or meaning?

punchline.text: Burnout has six roots. Cutting hours won't help if the real root is unfairness.

quiz.question: What is the most common cause of burnout according to Maslach?
options: Lack of control over how you do your job

details.summary: Christina Maslach identified six organizational factors that drive burnout: workload, lack of control, insufficient reward, absence of community, unfairness, and value conflicts. When multiple factors are present simultaneously, burnout risk escalates dramatically.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding the six causes shifts the focus from individual weakness to systemic issues. This framework helps organizations design targeted interventions that address root causes.
takeaways: Burnout has six organizational drivers, not one single cause
Value conflicts between personal and employer beliefs amplify risk
Addressing even two or three causes measurably reduces burnout

faq.question: Which of the six causes is the most common driver of burnout?
faq.answer: Research consistently identifies excessive workload as the most prevalent driver across industries. However, lack of control and perceived unfairness are the strongest predictors of severe burnout because they erode a person's sense of agency.

faq.question: Can an individual fix burnout if the causes are organizational?
faq.answer: Individuals can mitigate some causes through boundary setting and job crafting, but systemic burnout requires organizational change. The most effective approach combines personal coping strategies with advocacy for structural improvements in workload and fairness.
